rationale: This program is a tightly-coupled floating-point benchmark harness (whetstone/fbench/flops/FFT kernels) with only two tiny functions and 384 bytes of text, so the dominant constraint is runtime overhead on hot FP loops plus preserving numerically-verifiable correctness, while the tiny code surface limits how much any pass can diversify. SUB is the workhorse: it is cheap, correctness-preserving, and directly obscures the arithmetic identity of FP kernels, so it gets the highest SecurityGain and lowest risk/cost weights. FLA and IGV follow as medium-strong contributors: flattening complicates the loop/branch structure that a reverse engineer would anchor on, and IGV adds value-level diversity at modest cost; both are held back slightly on RuntimeCost/SizeCost because hot-loop dispatch overhead is real. SPLIT is enabled with mid weights as a cheap enabler that increases block-level diversity and gives other passes more blocks to transform. BCF and IBR are kept but with strongly damped RuntimeCost/SizeCost weights since bogus control flow and indirect branching are the most expensive transformations per executed edge in inner loops; they should only fire on features that indicate low execution frequency. ICALL is the weakest: this code is dominated by straight-line FP arithmetic with few call sites, indirect-call rewriting adds a runtime multiplier exactly where the program is most sensitive, and it carries the highest CorrectnessRisk weight (0.25) to keep it off FP-critical paths; it is retained only for its diversity contribution on the harness/driver code.
